newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM to seek approval for republican vote.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM to seek approval for republican vote.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard will seek party approval on Tuesday for a people's convention by year-end to consider whether the nation should become a republic, with a vote possible by the 1999 election.

Howard's cabinet has already approved the convention which would consider how Australia's constitutional monarchy can become a republic, replacing Britain's Queen Elizabeth with an Australian head-of-state, government sources said on Monday.
The prime minister is due to seek party-room approval for the plan on Tuesday, the sources said.

The move comes after recent fears that Howard, a staunch monarchist, was planning to abandon his 1996 election pledge to hold the convention this year and for half its delegates to be publicly elected. The remaining delegates would be appointed by the national and state governments.
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer on Monday would not say when an announcement on the convention would be made, but reaffirmed the government's commitment to its election promise.

"The core commitments of a convention, properly comprised, and a fair-dinkum (genuine) vote of the people, which we took to the elections last March, will definitely be provided," Fischer said in a radio interview.
"There will be no breaking of that word," FIscher said.
Opinion polls show about half of Australian voters want a republic, but also that they think the country faces more pressing problems. Many are uncommitted.
Support for a republic has grown as Australia's immigration intake shifts away from its traditional reliance on Britain as a source of new settlers.

Australia's former Labor government, ousted by Howard last year, fuelled the republic issue under outspoken prime minister Paul Keating. Keating, once condemned by the British media as the "Lizard of Oz" for touching the Queen, sought to establish a republic before the centenary of federation in 2001.

Howard's conservative Liberal-National coalition reluctantly agreed to take the issue to voters by the turn of the century and to involve the community in early consideration of the issue if it won government.
The A$50 million (US$38 million) people's convention will produce options for a republic to be voted on in a national plebiscite, but this vote would not be binding on the government.
The result of the plebiscite would form the basis of a national referendum, which would have to be passed by a majority of voters in a majority of the six states to change the constitution.
If the convention is held in December, as is now expected, the referendum could be held before or with the next national election due in March, 1999.
Republican leaders and media reports had warned Howard was delaying the consideration of a republic and considering having all convention delegates appointed by government.
The Labor opposition on Monday urged Howard to "junk" the convention and put the issue to a direct popular vote, accusing the prime minister of trying to sabotage the process.
"I don't think Mr Howard wants a republic and this is a way of unmercifully prolonging the process to ensure that it doesn't happen," deputy opposition leader Gareth Evans said.
New South Wales state opposition leader Peter Collins, a republican member of Howard's Liberal party, warned last week of a growing perception that Howard was abandoning his pledge.
